projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with William Minner was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So, go ahead.

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: My name is William Minner. I was born January 12th, 1920. Born in a little country store that -- my dad had a country store at Mastin's Corner, which is halfway between Felton and Harrington.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now where did you go to school?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: I went to school at Mastin's Corner for five years and they closed the country school down and I went there -- finished up at Harrington. After that I went to Goldie. It's -- it was Goldie and Beacon and now -- I went to Goldie for nine months and I knew more than the teacher knew so I -- I just quit.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did you -- where did you live up there?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: I lived --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did you --

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: I lived at a house on -- rented a room on 12th Street in Wilmington.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: My mom -- my mom and her sister, they all -- my mother and my aunt went to Goldie.

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Is that right?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Yep, right before -- it had been before the war.

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: It was '38 when I went there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Yeah, right about that same time and they were up at -- they lived at Ninth and Washington right across from Cosie Corner.

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Yeah. There were -- there were some -- there were some -- a couple of girls from Harrington that went and they lived on that street. I don't know where. There were maybe eight or ten of us went -- living in different places went there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So what were you studying at -- what were you studying there?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Just a general --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Business?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Just a general --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Business school? Business?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Business. Business. That's all I know. I don't remember too much about it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now did you --

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Nine months.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You went to --

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: I know that I didn't go to school enough to do any good, you know, get cut free from mother and father. And I did what I wanted to do -- or not what I wanted, but some things that I shouldn't have done. Oh, here you got me confessing my sins to my wife.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: We'll cut it out of the tape and we'll zap her before she goes. Did you play -- did you play sports?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Yeah, I played sports. I played basketball, soccer, and baseball.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Soccer?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Yeah, soccer. We didn't even have -- we didn't have football in our school. It wasn't big enough in Harrington to have soccer -- I mean, to have football.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So you played soccer and basketball. Were you a good basketball player?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Soccer, basketball, and baseball.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did you like playing basketball?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Did I like it? Yeah, I loved it. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: That was Harrington High?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Harrington High.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Which I think my great grandfather might have built.

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Beg your pardon?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: I think my great grandfather might have built Harrington High.

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Is that right?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Because I know we re-did the school.

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Yeah, well, it was -- it was an old school but they built on to it before I went there but it was an old school. We had to do our dressing and undressing down in the cellar where there were no heat or no -- nothing but just a boiler room down there so --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did --

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: -- things were pretty rough.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did -- did -- now, where were -- tell me about Pearl Harbor day? Do you remember Pearl Harbor day?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Tell me about what happened? Where -- where -- what you remember about Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Well, I wasn't -- I wasn't in the service then.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: No, I know, but tell me what you were doing? Do you remember what you were doing?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Well, yeah. It was on a Sunday morning, I believe, if I'm correct, and getting ready to go to church and when -- when I heard -- I guess maybe it was maybe after lunch, or something, but that's when I heard it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Were you -- were you home then or were you up at Goldie?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: No, I was home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You were back home?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: And what made you go to the service? Did you --

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: I went into the service May the 17th of 1943.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. You say you stayed out pretty much a year?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: I was -- I was -- I -- I -- I was discharged on December the 1st of '43. I got --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You were discharged --

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: I was discharged from the Army.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- in '46? Five?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: In -- in '45.

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: I went -- I was -- got on the boat in San Francisco to go overseas on December the 1st of '43 and I landed in Australia, Brisbane-Ascot. It's -- it's a racetrack. We were there -- we stayed there for a little while and then we went on to -- we were replacements is what our shipload was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What branch of the service were you in?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: I was in the Army. I was a PFC and then they jumped me to tech sergeant. Before we left they wanted to make me a lieutenant and I said, no, I don't want that responsibility. Just before I left they asked -- came to me and said would you then take a lieutenant's job for a year if we made you lieutenant? I said, you couldn't make me a captain and keep me back here. I want to go home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, where were you stationed then? When you were overseas, what -- what -- what battles were you in? Were you in battles?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Yeah. We had -- we had training to get -- we were assigned to our different companies and regiments -- regiments and we -- then we're -- we're starting to do basic -- undergo basic training all over again from where we were before we got to -- before we got to California we were at Macon, Georgia. That was where I was __ -- was -- was -- took my training in Macon, Georgia, and then they sent us to California to hit the boat. And we got there. And then when we got in Australia, we were sent to a place called Rockhampton. It was hot. Oh, everyplace I went was hot. I never -- I never had -- had to wear any clothes hardly at all. In Makin, Georgia, it is hot in the summertime. Anyway, then after we got through training in Rockhampton where they put us on a boat to go to Hollandia in Dutch New Guinea. {Coughing} -- excuse me. We -- they expected a big fight but there wasn't any Japs that we could see anyplace. But then when we started coming to land they put us in this, like an LST, but drops the front of it down and you -- you run out in the water so deep, you know. And the Japs were back inland further and they were in caves. They had beautiful rooms in -- dug in in caves and there's no way we could do -- do anything but just -- when they -- when they came out of these caves maybe they have -- we had a flame thrower that shot fire into the caves and that's how we could get them in the daytime. At nighttime that's when they tried to get us. They would send men out on patrol and so forth. And we had to -- two men to a hole, to a foxhole and one man would stay awake for an hour, then he would go to sleep and then the other guy would. All night long it was like that. First one hour and then -- then -- it never did get any longer than that, but you prayed for -- I prayed for it to get dark and then I prayed for it to get light. And it was just tough going for a while.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now what battle was that?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: That was the Battle of Biak, B-i-a-k. It was -- it was tough. They -- those caves, they had sinkholes, too, built in a triangle. Then they had walkways in between and they let us walk right into that triangle and then they opened fire on us. My sergeant got killed standing on the side of me and I hit the dirt and had to lay on my belly until it got dark because every time we moved, they'd shoot at us. And we stayed there -- I forget how long it was, if it's, oh, close to a year, I guess, and then I got typhus. There was a lot of malaria. Everybody -- a lot of the people got malaria. You'd take a little pill and it would turn you yellow. And you could tell if a new man come in in your outfit, he'd be white. We were all yellow. And I --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now how long did that battle go on there in that island?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: It -- it went on close to two years, I guess. I can't remember exactly. In my magazine or my book that I got, it tells us how long we were there, where we went, and so forth.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Where did you go after that?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: After that we went to Palawan. We -- the reason we went there is we got a report that we had -- that we had some Air Force boys in -- in Palawan that they shot down and we were gonna go try to capture Japs, or get rid of them, so we -- so we could get the boys. And before we got there they had poured gasoline on all of them in a hole and set fire to them and burned them up. And then we went on patrolling around the -- around the island and we -- there was another small island next to Palawan, and I forget the name of it, and we cleaned it out of Japs. And then I guess we came back -- came back to high ground again almost -- I don't know. I don't remember that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: After Palawan --

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: I was -- I was in -- I -- I got typhus. I didn't get malaria for -- right then. I got typhus while I was on Biak and they didn't have penicillin then. And all the men and boys that would die from peni- -- from typhus -- I had a big -- they put a big boy, about six foot four, weighed 200 and some pounds in the bed next to me and in about ten days he was dead. They just were dropping off like flies. I was in -- I was there for 30 days, lost 30 pounds, and then I went -- went back to my company and kept on fighting.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How about after Palawan, where did you go after that?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Palawan?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Palawan, after Palawan?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Palawan?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: After that?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: After Palawan is -- Palawan.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: How about your last --

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: I guess -- I guess it was -- we got to Zamboanga and we -- we didn't -- we didn't have to do anything. That was a resting station back there. And, of course, that old saying of Zamboanga, the monkeys has no tails, but I don't believe that was right. But we were there when the war was over. We were having prac- -- gun shooting practice down coconut -- rows of coconut trees. And we were shooting at the target and word came that the war was over. We started shooting everything. Coconuts coming down, falling down all around you. And the Army didn't like that so they took the pay out of our check -- out of our pay for doing that. I thought that was nice of them to do that. Then we -- then we went to Hiroshima where they dropped that first bomb. And I just didn't -- maybe Hiroshima was about the size of Wilmington, you know, but there was never more than one side of a building standing. And it was tough. Nobody could come out of it alive. They cleaned her up. And then we -- our job was taking all of their -- all of their artillery, their guns, and everything, put them on a boat, take them out to sea and dump them overboard and that's what we did. And then that's -- then I -- I stayed there for, I don't know, a couple months and it was my time to come back home. So I got on the boat December the 1st again to come home. I was there just three years. And I got back to -- to California, got on a train to go to Fort Dix, New Jersey, to get discharged. And before we got to Chicago on the train I got malaria and I got a bad high fever and they stopped the train and put me in the hospital. I didn't get malaria the whole time I was there fighting, to get -- but I got it there. And then I stayed there a couple of three days. They sent me on to Camp Dix to get my discharge and I got discharged and came home.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What did you do when you got back?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Nothing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Nothing?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Just -- just loafed. I loafed around, oh, for over -- maybe just about 30 days doing what I wanted to do. Nothing or sleep or whatever I wanted.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Did your family have the store then still?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: They -- they still had the store. Shortly after that they -- they -- they had closed the store. He was getting older and my mother. Those two took care of it all their lives just about. And I got a job with a Danny Dupont (ph) in Seaford where it was a Godsent for all -- all of us boys getting jobs coming back at that time. And I worked there, I don't know, a couple of years. And I had various jobs in between, which I didn't like, and finally I got a job with the state. I was a liquor agent for the state and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: A.B.C.?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: For two -- three -- two years and then I -- they promoted me to the chief. And I was a chief until I retired in 1980. March the 12th, 1980, I retired. I've been retired ever since.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: I bet that was a good job?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Beg your pardon?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: I bet that was a good job?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Well, it was. It was -- It wasn't hard. It was just long hours. You work at nighttime, daytime. We only had nine men, including myself.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Through the whole state?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: For the whole state.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: That's probably when I was --

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: I was -- that's probably when I was sneaking in buying beer when I was 17 years old.

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Well, I had --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: I wish I had known that information then.

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: I had two daughters to go to Delaware and we -- you could go over there and pick up, you know, all the college kids. And I was sure that my youngest daughter, I was sure I'd catch her. But she -- she didn't -- she didn't get caught, but --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Yeah, we used to go over up on that -- out on that road out -- out past -- what was the name of that place? Zerbern (ph), Maryland. You could go over there up at that place, run over the state line and get the liquor.

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: No, we just -- we -- we would find out when they were gonna have a big dance or something, you know, and go up there and we never -- never tried to -- well, if they -- if they were underage we would take them maybe get in touch with their teacher or their -- whoever was in charge.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Scare the hell out of them?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Now, where did you meet your wife?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Where did I meet her? I met her at a -- Shall I tell him? I met her at a bar in Harrington.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Nice.

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: A place called the Wonder Oar (ph). And that's where all of the returnees were going at -- at that time. She was from Milford and they -- some Milford girls used to come over and we would dance with them and so forth and so on. I met -- that's where I met her and -- and we went -- went -- I -- I guess we went a year maybe before we got married and we got married February the 28th of -- the last day of February in -- in 1940- -- '48. And we've been married ever since.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Very nice.

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: We lived -- we -- we -- my father built us a house in Harrington and we lived there until -- we had a cellar and an upstairs and we got to the point where it was just -- everything was downstairs, the washing machine, dryers, and so forth, and we just decided we'd __ + we try and get a one-floor house. So right outside of Harrington towards Milford they made a place -- a fellow sold his farm to a builder to build houses and he built this house and we liked it. We bought it and moved in there in 1999. 19- -- yeah, I think that's right, 1990. It wasn't 2000 yet. That's all -- 1990, I guess. And here I am right here waiting.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: {Laughing.} Now did your -- did you work at -- I'm talking to your wife now. Were you -- what did you do during the war?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Minner
sp.p: I was at the University of Delaware --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Minner
sp.p: -- at the time and I can remember we've been out someplace that Sunday and came back for Sunday night supper, you know, and they told us about Pearl -- Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: When did you start at Delaware?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Minner
sp.p: I started in 1940, September of '40. Graduated in December of '43, plus we went through the accelerated program.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Minner
sp.p: I said I was so smart I got out in three years and three months, but that wasn't true. I did get out in three years and three months, but I wasn't very smart.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Well, you must of had smarter teachers there than he had up at Goldie?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Minner
sp.p: Well, he went to Goldie on a -- just to play basketball.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Oh. Those guys always had a good basketball team.

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: I mean, up 'til just recently -- I mean, you know, they had --

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Oh, yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: They had some top -- top-notch players.

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: We played -- we played some young -- some young -- some freshman college people when I was in high school playing soccer. My coach came from Westchester. He was -- he -- as a -- as a soccer player and a coach and every year we'd go back and play their JV team. In my four years of soccer playing we beat them all four years. They -- they had a good team, but we had -- we had one -- we very seldom lost a game in hockey -- or in soccer.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Why don't we get -- you want to get a picture of him with his uniform?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Yeah, sure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: We'll do that.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: But we need to swing the microphone over here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Okay. All right. What we're going to do is just take a picture of you with your -- holding up your uniform.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: I have a question also.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Oh, go ahead. I'm sorry.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: When you came to Hiroshima, was it completely empty? Were there any people left?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: When you went to Hiroshima, how -- were there any people left there at all?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Oh, there were a few. Not a whole lot. They were coming back. But when they dropped that bomb they killed practically everybody that was there. There -- I don't remember exactly how -- how many but I know there was nothing standing except the side of a building here and a side there. Never a whole building of any kind. And they were -- they were coming -- they were coming back in and starting to build up.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: And for me as a civilian who -- who -- who's born way after this, it's just fascinating that -- were they angry or were they just, like, defeated at this point?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: I didn't get that.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Were the -- were they -- were the people -- the -- the -- were the Japanese that were there, were they -- did -- were they angry or did they --

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Oh, they were nice to us. They -- they -- they did anything we wanted them to do. They -- didn't have to worry about taking -- carrying your gun or just -- they were -- well, they were all right. They were just good people trying to come back in.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Minner
sp.p: Tell them about the warehouse of rice.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: The warehouse full of rice?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Oh. Yeah, we ran across that and it was our job to make -- staying guard over that so there wasn't much more. All of the other jobs was taking all the fighting instruments out into the sea or in the ocean and dump them overboard so they wouldn't be able to use them again.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Was anybody concerned about the radiation or anything from the bomb --

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: No. No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: -- left over or nothing?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Not that I know of.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Minner
sp.p: He said the pictures that they took never could be developed so there must have been radiation.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Oh, you -- that's interesting. The pictures you took, were those already exposed or overexposed?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: When you took pictures --

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Where are the pictures? Yeah, I took some but I had a jet camera and I didn't have any film. I only had one roll. I used that up and I lost them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You lost them or was there enough radiation there that screwed the -- screwed the film up?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: No, I lost them. I lost them there someplace. I don't know just where. And I wasn't really too concerned about it anyway. I should have been more concerned because, you know, that's something that's not going to happen, I hope, again, but --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Minner
sp.p: I thought he said that the film was no good but.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: I got my dad's.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Minner
sp.p: He's been mayor of Harrington.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Oh, oh.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Minner
sp.p: On city counsel and two terms as mayor.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: What was your last term as mayor?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: What was what?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Your last term as mayor down at Harrington? When were you the mayor? What -- what -- how long were you the mayor?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: I was the mayor of two terms, six years. And I served a three-year term as a --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Minner
sp.p: Council.

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: As a representative. Then I was elected mayor two times, six years, and that was enough for the job that I had and trying keep things going.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Minner
sp.p: {Laughing.}

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: So you were still in A.B.C. then?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: I was doing -- I was -- I was working for the A.B.C., yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You got the slots in anyway.

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Did what, sir?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You got the slots in.

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Oh, yeah, they got the slots. Yeah, I had race horses too but when they got to playing big money I went out of business. I just couldn't -- couldn't afford to buy those high-priced horses and taking a chance, so I didn't do it. I sold everything.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You, apparently, weren't in the lottery down there. I thought -- I thought the tale was that if you were down on your luck you'd win the next race and they'd win the next race and --

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: I used to go up at Brandywine. I was at Brandywine all the time.

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Oh. I don't -- I don't know. I -- I don't know.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Do you want to do this?

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Yeah, but what you do with this?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You want to just hold it up.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Hold it up?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You can hold it up in front of him.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: You think?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Yeah. Okay.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Why don't you just -- you can just hold -- yeah, hold that out like that. That's good.

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Like that?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Yeah, that's good. Just -- let me just look over here.

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Higher?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: You're fine. That's good. My father worked down at Seaford right after the war.

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Sir?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: My father worked down at Seaford right when he got back from World War Two.

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: Oh, is that right?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: He graduated from -- he was at Delaware in '38.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Minner
sp.p: Oh, was he?

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Well that whole gang, 198 Coast Artillery that were in the ROTC up there.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Minner
sp.p: I was right there when they all went. I was there when the ASTP people were there, too. They took a lot of young men that were college level and they were gonna train them to be officers, but the Battle of the Bulge happened and they all went there. But it was fun. We had a lot of --

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: Don't hang up your service flag, mother, your son's in the ASTP.

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: I don't -- I don't think so. I don't -- I don't know. I don't remember

sp.speaker: Mrs. Minner
sp.p: I didn't know him then.

sp.speaker: Unidentified Speaker
sp.p: Okay. Thank you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Healy
sp.p: That's good. That didn't hurt, did it?

sp.speaker: William Minner
sp.p: No. (End of Interview.)
